claims.text: The studied particles are initially solid, equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles form a single-phase solid solution.
The controlled intervention compares slow cooling at about 1 K/min with faster cooling at about 10 K/min.
Particle size distribution and defect density are to be controlled while particles are heated in TEM from below premelting through complete melting.
Slower cooling provides sufficient surface-atom mobility for diffusion and local rearrangement.
Slower cooling enables incipient local chemical ordering or segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface rearrangement, ordering, or segregation lowers or otherwise modulates local surface energy.
Lower local surface energy promotes localized premelting before the bulk melting transition.
Rapid cooling preserves a high-entropy, homogeneous single-phase state by kinetically suppressing secondary-phase formation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous solid solution during rapid cooling and effectively freezes in chemical disorder.
Slow-cooled particles will begin surface premelting at a lower temperature than fast-cooled particles.
Slow-cooled particles will exhibit more spatially heterogeneous premelting with localized liquid-like regions.
Fast-cooled particles will undergo a more uniform melting transition at higher temperatures.
The fast-cooled baseline retains a relatively unaltered homogeneous solid-solution state.
The proposed mechanism applies only over particle sizes and defect levels for which surface diffusion dominates the response.
Particle-size variations and pre-existing defects may independently affect melting behavior.
Failure to observe a statistically significant earlier or more heterogeneous premelting response after slow cooling would refute the proposed cooling-rate effect.
